summary.text: Female patient with refractory palmoplantar pustular psoriasis (PPPP) diagnosed 33 years earlier and concomitant psoriatic arthritis and fibromyalgia. Prior acitretin with psoralen-UVA, methotrexate and cyclosporine A were not tolerated and were discontinued. Figure 2 shows numerous pustules on scaled red skin at baseline. Her smoking history was positive and baseline PGA was 3.

Apremilast was started and titrated to 30 mg 2x/d. Five weeks after initiation her PsA improved substantially and PPPP was scored PGA 1; Figure 2 shows partial remission and reduced inflammation after 5 weeks. Mild gastrointestinal side effects were reported for all six patients of the series.

At the follow-up visit after 5 months she had a PPPP relapse following discontinuation of apremilast 3 weeks earlier. Several days after apremilast was re-administered she reached PGA 1, stable at subsequent visits; Table 1 lists an endpoint PGA of 1 after 18 months of follow-up.

summary.text: Female patient with refractory palmoplantar pustular psoriasis (PPPP) diagnosed 7 years before presentation, with psoriatic arthritis, arterial hypertension, depression, obesity and type II diabetes. Acitretin, psoralen-UVA, cyclosporine A, adalimumab, ustekinumab and secukinumab did not improve her skin lesions and biologics were stopped for adverse effects. Baseline PGA was 4, with numerous conflating pustules on the left sole (Figure 3).

Apremilast was started and titrated to 30 mg 2x/d. She reported rapid subjective relief of symptoms within several days. After 4 weeks pustules decreased in number and size and PGA improved from 4 to 2. Mild gastrointestinal side effects were reported for all six patients of the series.

After 3 months of apremilast and at all later follow-up visits she recorded PGA 1, and Figure 3 shows a substantial decrease of inflammation and pustules after 12 weeks. Table 1 lists the same endpoint PGA of 1 with 18 months of follow-up and a negative smoking history.

summary.text: Male patient with refractory palmoplantar pustular psoriasis (PPPP) diagnosed 6 years earlier, with depression and arterial hypertension listed in Table 1. Alitretinoin, acitretin, methotrexate and psoralen-UVA were not effective in inducing remission. He presented with severe PPPP, PGA 3, and a positive smoking history.

After apremilast initiation he reported significant subjective skin improvement within 10 days. The drug was discontinued after 4 months because of a depressive episode without suicidal ideation, followed by new pustules within 2 days. Mild gastrointestinal side effects were reported for all six patients.

After interdisciplinary psychiatric consultation apremilast was reintroduced, with major improvement of skin lesions within 1 week. He maintained PGA 1 at all following visits; Table 1 lists endpoint PGA 1 after 18 months of follow-up.

summary.text: Female patient with refractory palmoplantar pustular psoriasis (PPPP) diagnosed 12 years previously and concomitant psoriatic arthritis. Previous treatments included oral glucocorticosteroids, psoralen-UVA, secukinumab, cyclosporine A, azathioprine and methotrexate. She had severe skin involvement, PGA 3, and a positive smoking history.

Apremilast was started and titrated to 30 mg 2x/d. Skin lesions improved to PGA 1 within 2 weeks of initiation, and pustules on the palms and soles resolved completely (PGA 0) at the week 12 follow-up visit. Mild gastrointestinal side effects were reported for all six patients.
Apremilast was subsequently discontinued because of her desire to have a child; Table 1 lists an endpoint PGA of 0 with 6 months of follow-up.

Prior oral glucocorticosteroids, methotrexate, psoralen-UVA, alitretinoin and acitretin were given. Her smoking history was positive.

Apremilast was started and titrated to 30 mg 2x/d. After initial paradoxical worsening of severe palmoplantar lesions to PGA 3, she improved to PGA 2 after 4 weeks. At the next visit PGA was 1 for the palms and 1–2 for the soles. Mild gastrointestinal side effects were reported for all six patients.
Her skin condition remained stable at PGA 1 for 18 months during ongoing apremilast treatment; Table 1 lists an endpoint PGA of 1 with 18 months of follow-up.

summary.text: Male patient with refractory palmoplantar pustular psoriasis (PPPP) diagnosed 6 years earlier, with psoriatic arthritis and depression. Prior acitretin, psoralen-UVA, methotrexate, cyclosporine A, oral corticosteroids and secukinumab were discontinued for lack of efficacy and/or adverse effects. Highly painful joint involvement led to prednisolone 10 mg/d around the start of apremilast.

Apremilast was started and titrated to 30 mg 2x/d. Four weeks after initiation PGA was 1. At the week 12 follow-up palms were PGA 2 with five pustules while the soles had no pustules and were PGA 0. Mild gastrointestinal side effects were reported for all six patients.

Apremilast was discontinued after 6 months because of an exacerbation of PsA, in order to initiate TNF-alpha inhibitor treatment. At discontinuation the soles were cleared and the palms PGA 1; Table 1 lists the endpoint as 0 for soles and 1 for palms with 6 months of follow-up.

article_limitations: Ages differ between the Results paragraphs and Table 1 for all six patients (one digit for five, a larger gap for patient 3); all age facts are review_only and no age appears in labels or summaries.

Table 2 drug lists differ from the text for patient 2 (ETN, methotrexate and glucocorticosteroids marked in the table only; secukinumab named in the text only); ETN is not expanded in the table footnote.

Cohort aggregate statements about PGA at 4 weeks and 12 weeks (b00022) are not copied to individuals and do not exactly match the individual paragraphs (for example more than one patient at PGA 2 at 4 weeks individually, and palms PGA 2 for patient 6 at week 12 against two PGA 0 patients in the aggregate).
Patient 6 week 12 text says disease activity decreased to PGA 2 after PGA 1 at four weeks.
Figure 1 values are pixel content and kept in visual.json only; its legend labels the end of observation as 18 months although two patients were followed 6 months.
Disease duration in Table 1 equals the text diagnosis intervals; it was not added as separate facts.
Abstract and methods follow-up statements (four patients 18 months, two 6 months) are not attributed to individuals except through Table 1 per-case rows.

Parent decision: Table 1/Table 2 'Case N' rows are attributed to text 'Patient N' by the article's own identical numbering of its six-patient series (figure captions also say 'patient 1'/'patient 2'); this is a printed label, not attribute matching, and sex, disease duration and comorbidities agree. The source never states the mapping explicitly.

Five of six Table 1 ages exceed the text age by exactly one year, which may reflect different reference times that the source does not state; kept as ambiguities. Patient 3 (54 vs 48) is a source conflict.
Figure 1 prints a single end-of-observation label 0 for patient 6, while Table 1 gives 0 (soles) 1 (palms); pixel values stay in visual.json only.
